job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Fatima Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's busy, I like it. I share a rented room near the campus in Mirador with my sister Lucia, who's finishing her last year, and I'm at the family bakery by six on weekends to do the books and the online orders. I studied business at Mirador University and passed with an average result, no internship. I use AI tools every day, for invoices, for the bakery's menu, even for writing the shop's social posts. During the week I apply for junior roles in operations and finance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then the tools I've learned stay useful and nothing changes for small businesses like ours. I'd tell people to use the practical bits and ignore the promises. A bakery doesn't run on hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'd still be applying, still running the bakery's books, which is real work. I think a lot about whether I should just build the bakery's online business and not chase a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to 10 or 12 roles a week, and in parallel I'd turn the bakery's online orders into a proper delivery service, with a simple website and a pickup schedule. I'd track every sale and cost in a clean sheet, so I can show a firm what I did. And I'd ask my father for a small budget for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, confident. I know I can do real work, I just need the first stamp from a firm. But I'm not desperate, because the bakery means I'm always doing something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use AI a lot. Would it change anything if it stalled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, because I've got no internship and an average result, and firms that rank on those two things don't even open the file. I can't change that. I can change what's in the file, which is why the bakery figures matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why no offer yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would not change much. The tools help with the boring parts, and my customers still want bread made by a person they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expect, and we should adapt, not complain. Small businesses should learn the tools, and the government should make training cheap. Free markets will sort it out if people have skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm slightly uneasy. Entry roles in finance and operations are exactly where AI helps firms save. But I think I'd be among those who can use it, so I'd be fine, if I'm quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd roll out online ordering and AI-based stock planning at the bakery within six months. I'd offer the same setup to three nearby shops, for a small fee. I'd apply to firms that build small-business tools, since I'm basically their customer. And I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a little nervous. It's like opening a new shop, you know it can go well, but it's yours to make it so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does a bakery change in a world like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bakery's costs are flour, butter, rent, wages and waste. AI helps with waste and ordering, so we make fewer loaves that get thrown away. That alone could pay for the setup in a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slow adopters. My father is great, but he'd rather use a notebook. I worry he'll resist, and that the bakery will get left behind. So I'd need to show him, not tell him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be calm and practical. Governments should keep the economy running and help people work, not just pay them. I'd say that businesses and families will have to carry a lot, so help them early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious. If AI does all thinking work, junior finance roles vanish, and the tools I've mastered are now cheap for everyone. But the bakery makes bread, and people will buy bread from a person for a while. It's not a plan forever, but it buys time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put all my effort into the bakery, expanding the online side and maybe opening a second counter. I'd cut my personal spending and put money aside. I'd keep an eye out for a good job, but I'd rather own something. I'd also ask my father to start documenting recipes and processes, in case we need to scale or sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, a bit scared. It feels like being on a boat when the wind changes. You can't stop the wind, but you can adjust the sails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Lucia, don't panic and don't wait. Finish your last year, and consider something hands-on. She'd say she's not sure, and we'd probably argue, then make tea. And we'd call our parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the bakery survive 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes. Until robots can bake and deliver at scale, about 2031, a small family bakery has a human edge. After that, it's less clear, so I'd use the time to build a brand people like.

Businesses and families will carry a lot, so help them early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent window. Businesses should train staff, schools should teach tools and money skills, and the state should keep taxes light so firms can invest. I'd say it to anyone running a shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm hopeful. In five years I could own a small group of bakery shops, or have a role in a firm that builds tools for them. Either way I'd be using AI more than most. The risk is moving too slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job in operations or finance for the experience, and keep growing the bakery on weekends. I'd invest in better ovens and online systems. I'd save about 40 percent of my income. And I'd learn to manage people, which no AI tool does for you yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but driven. It's like training for a race with a known date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. How do you use the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not put everything into one thing. If robots get into baking, we'd need something else, like the brand, or a cafe space. I'd diversify early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I can do both, learn at a firm and grow our own place. With two I'd have to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great runway. Let businesses build, let people retrain, and keep government support simple and temporary. A decade is long enough to prepare properly if we start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm excited. At 33 I could own a few shops, have a family, and be well placed in the AI economy. I might even sell tools to other bakeries. It could be a good decade for people willing to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for a firm for a couple of years, build the bakery's online side, then go full-time in the family business and expand. I'd invest in property for the shops instead of renting. I'd save, and I'd keep learning every new tool as it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit thrilled. I'd rather have ten years to build than be surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What does your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Complacency. Plenty of people hear ten years and relax. I'd write down yearly goals and review them every December, with my sister, who'd hold me to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly no, and I'd tell younger people the same. Own something, learn something, save something. That's enough for a decade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time to build the brand and the online side before everything shifts. What would help is simple rules, cheap training for small business owners, and a way to keep bread local and human a bit longer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm optimistic, but I know I'm lucky to be. A family business, no debt, and tools I like. Other people my age might not have that, and plans should think of them.

headlineQuote: I'm optimistic, but I know I'm lucky to be. A family business, no debt, and tools I like.
portrait: Fatima is a **23-year-old** business graduate sharing a room with her sister, doing the family bakery's books and online orders.
She is **traditional** and free-market: she values family, ownership and skills over handouts.
She is **adaptive**, uses AI every day and wants to modernise the bakery.
Her bakery turns every scenario into a question of ownership; she is **calm** when she has time and anxious when she doesn't.
She says plainly that her luck is not shared by everyone her age.
biggestWorry: Her biggest worry is **AGI by 2028**, which leaves no time to build the brand and online side.
whatWouldHelp: Simple rules, **cheap training** for small business owners, and ways to keep local bread human a bit longer.
